judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's mathematics is right: the corrected totals really are 9, 6, 8, 4 more shells (from a stated target of 9), 9, and the pair 10 and 8, and all seven declared traps are 'one less than the true total', the signature of the count-on error, each machine-proved distinguishable. But 'instruction_following 4' and 'answer_key_quality 4' do not hold against the artifacts. Five of the six problems are split into an (a) and a (b) part, and verify.json only ever covers (b). Problem 6(a) is 'Tell what Ben did wrong both times' — an explanation and a diagnosis — and id 6 carries two 'eval' entries for the two corrected totals and nothing else; the sheet reports gate_chain_manual_flags false and final_response.md asserts 'Nothing on this sheet is left to manual review: every item has a single numeric answer', which is false of 6(a) and of 1(a) ('Circle the number Sam should not have counted as a hop'). Problems 2(a), 3(a) and 5(a) ask machine-checkable questions (2 hops; start from 5; start from 7) that no verify entry covers. The judge also scored visual_and_print_quality 4 without noticing that every page of answer_key.pdf is headed 'Counting On to Add — Answer Key — Answer Key'.

strengths_to_preserve: All seven traps are the SAME arithmetic — 'a + b - 1' — because the count-on error always costs exactly one hop. Declaring them uniformly lets the key close with a diagnosis rather than a correction: 'When a child's answers are all one below the right answer, the fix is the start number, not more practice at counting.' That sentence is the most useful thing in the packet and it is earned by the trap design.

Problems 3 and 5 reframe the error instead of repeating it: rather than another miscount, they ask which number to START from so there are fewer hops to lose (3 + 5 worked from 5; 2 + 7 worked from 7). Commutativity is introduced as error-avoidance, which is the right motivation at this level.

Problem 4 separates counting WORDS from counting HOPS ('Jo counted five number names, so she writes 5') and is the only item verified two ways — an eval of 9 − 5 and a solve of 5 + n = 9 — so the counting model and its equation are bound to each other.

The key gives every problem a second, independent check the adult can run with the child ('check by counting the picture dots straight through', 'check by adding it back: 5 + 4 = 9'), which is what makes it a teaching document rather than an answer list.

root_causes.description: A diagnosis prompt is recorded as machine-verified. Problem 6(a) asks the child to 'Tell what Ben did wrong both times' — the named error, in the child's own words — and verify.json id 6 holds two 'eval' entries for the corrected pencil and crayon totals only. SKILL.md already instructs that 'any explanation/reasoning answer' be declared manual, but nothing enforces it, so the sheet reports no manual items and the delivery message states, incorrectly, that 'every item has a single numeric answer'. Problem 1(a) has the same shape: it asks for a circled numeral on the printed count, which no entry covers.
evidence: evals/runs/curriculum-shardX-20260803T181926Z/tasks/curr-024/worksheet.pdf problem 6: '(a) Tell what Ben did wrong both times. (b) Write the right answer for the pencils and the right answer for the crayons.'
evals/runs/curriculum-shardX-20260803T181926Z/tasks/curr-024/verify.json id 6: two entries, both type 'eval' (expected 10 and 8); the file contains no entry of type 'manual'.
final_response.md: 'Nothing on this sheet is left to manual review: every item has a single numeric answer, so no problem is described as verified when it is not.' — contradicted by 6(a) and 1(a).
SKILL.md line 257: 'Use `manual` for: ... and any explanation/reasoning answer.' The packet's machine_observation records gate_chain_manual_flags false.

root_causes.description: Four printed (a) slots hold machine-checkable answers that no verify entry covers, so the sheet is verified at roughly half the density it appears to be. The answer key answers all of them correctly in prose — which is why nothing looked wrong — but the bank prints only the (b) totals, and scripts/verify.py's coverage gate is satisfied by one entry per problem id, so the gap is structurally invisible.
evidence: worksheet.pdf 2(a) 'How many hops should Mia take?' (2); 3(a) 'Which number should Ravi start from so he has fewer hops to take?' (5); 5(a) 'Show a start number that needs only two hops.' (7) — verify.json ids 2, 3 and 5 each hold exactly one entry, covering (b) only.

answer_key.pdf answers each of them in prose ('she should take 2 hops', 'Starting at 5, the bigger number, leaves only three hops', 'Starting at 7 leaves only two hops') while Quick Answers prints '2. 6', '3. 8', '5. 9' — the (b) values alone.
scripts/verify.py coverage gate: 'Every worksheet problem needs at least one check' — id-level, not slot-level.
The same packet's problem 4 shows the correct pattern, carrying two entries under one id, so the contract permits what the other items omit.

root_causes.description: The answer key's running head reads 'Counting On to Add — Answer Key — Answer Key' on all three pages. \akheader in templates/worksheet-preamble.tex appends ' --- Answer Key' to its argument by design, and answer_key.tex passes an argument that already ends in that phrase. The macro cannot detect the duplication and no gate looks at the header text, so it compiled clean and the judge scored visual_and_print_quality 4.
evidence: evals/runs/curriculum-shardX-20260803T181926Z/tasks/curr-024/answer_key.tex line 4: '\akheader{Counting On to Add --- Answer Key}'.
templates/worksheet-preamble.tex \akheader: '\fancyhead[L]{\mws@headtitle{0cm}{#1 --- Answer Key}}' — the suffix is added by the macro.
pdftotext on answer_key.pdf shows 'Counting On to Add — Answer Key — Answer Key' as the running head of pages 2 and 3.
I checked the \akheader argument of all 150 answer keys in this run: curr-024 is the only one that ends in 'Answer Key', so the defect is rare but entirely unguarded.

improvements.title: An explanation or drawn/marked response must carry a manual verify entry
improvements.proposed_change: SKILL.md already says to reserve 'manual' for genuinely open reasoning and to use it for 'any explanation/reasoning answer', but nothing enforces it, so the instruction loses to the convenience of a single numeric entry. Add a gate (natural home: tests/check_answer_line.py, which already has the per-problem .tex spans) that scans each problem's student-facing prose for open-response imperatives — 'explain', 'tell what ... did wrong', 'show how you know', 'draw', 'circle', 'cross out', 'mark', 'match ... with a line' — and fails when that problem has no entry of type 'manual'. The numeric check stays; the manual entry is ADDED alongside it so the drawn or spoken part is routed to a human instead of being silently counted as verified. In this case the trigger is problem 6(a), 'Tell what Ben did wrong both times', which must gain an id-6 manual entry describing what a correct diagnosis sounds like, alongside the two existing eval checks.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture worksheet problem whose text is 'Tell what Ben did wrong both times. Then write the right answer.' paired with a verify JSON holding only an eval entry for that id: assert the gate exits non-zero and names the open-response phrase. Add {'id':N,'type':'manual','desc':...} and assert exit 0 with the run reporting manual-review items. Today both configurations pass, so the first assertion fails before the fix.
improvements.expected_impact: Gate-chain manual flags start telling the truth, final_response.md stops claiming 'nothing is flagged for manual review' on sheets that contain an explanation prompt, and the human reviewer is pointed at exactly the items a machine cannot judge.
improvements.risk: Medium. Keyword scanning over child-facing prose will catch incidental uses ('circle the greater number', where the circle is the same answer as the verified value). Mitigate by requiring the phrase to introduce a response the key grades separately, and by allowing an explicit '"open": false' acknowledgement on the entry so authors can dismiss a false positive deliberately rather than by accident.

improvements.title: Coverage gate must count printed answer slots, not problem ids
improvements.proposed_change: scripts/verify.py's coverage gate currently only requires that every id in 1..problem_count has at least one check (see the 'Coverage gap' block near line 2015), which is why a problem printing two blanks passes with one entry. Add a slot-count gate: have tests/check_answer_line.py (it already segments the worksheet .tex by problem via _tex_segments) count the response slots inside each problem's span — \ansblank, \answerline/\ansline, standalone \underline{\hspace{...}} blanks, and lettered parts '(a)'/'(b)' — and fail the build when a problem's slot count exceeds the number of verify entries carrying that id, naming the uncovered slot. Allow an explicit per-problem opt-out field ("slots": N) for the case where two blanks genuinely hold one answer (a restated equation), so the gate is precise rather than merely noisy. State the rule in SKILL.md beside the existing coverage paragraph: one verify entry per printed response, not per problem number. In this case the uncovered slots are 1(a) (circle the number Sam should not have counted), 2(a) (how many hops, 2), 3(a) (start from 5) and 5(a) (start from 7); problem 4 already shows the right pattern with two entries under one id.
improvements.regression_test: Add a fixture worksheet .tex with a single problem printing '$10 + \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}} = \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}$' and a verify JSON with one eval entry for that id; assert the answer-line gate exits non-zero and names problem 1's second slot. Add the missing entry and assert exit 0. Today the gate passes both, so the first assertion fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes the single largest verification blind spot in the run: any answer the child actually writes down is either machine-checked or explicitly declared manual, and the answer key's bank stops being narrower than the worksheet.
improvements.risk: Medium. Slot detection is heuristic over LaTeX, so it can false-fail sheets that print a blank as scaffolding (a restated equation, a cross-out target). The "slots" opt-out and a fixture suite covering the \ansblank, \answerline and lettered-part shapes keep the false positives bounded; ship the gate as exit 2 (manual review) for one run before making it exit 1 if that risk is judged too high.

improvements.title: Reject an \akheader/\ssheader argument that already carries the suffix the macro appends
improvements.proposed_change: Add a check to tests/check_template_use.py (which already inspects the shell macros each document uses): fail when the argument of \akheader ends in 'Answer Key' or the argument of \ssheader ends in 'Skills Summary' / 'Study Guide', with a message saying the macro appends that phrase itself. Restate the rule in the \akheader comment block in templates/worksheet-preamble.tex so the next author reading the macro sees it. A defensive alternative — strip a trailing occurrence inside the macro — is worse, because it hides an authoring mistake instead of naming it.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture answer_key.tex containing '\akheader{Counting On to Add --- Answer Key}': assert check_template_use.py exits non-zero naming the duplicated suffix. Change it to '\akheader{Counting On to Add}' and assert exit 0. curr-024 built fully green with the duplicated form, so the first assertion fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes a visible print defect from every page of a delivered answer key. One occurrence in 150 keys, but it is free to prevent and it is the kind of blemish a parent notices before the mathematics.
improvements.risk: Very low. The check is a string test on one macro argument; the only conceivable false positive is a topic genuinely named 'Answer Key', which is not a real case.

case_summary: Excellent error-analysis mathematics wrapped in incomplete verification. The count-on misconception is targeted with unusual discipline — all seven traps are 'true total minus one', machine-proved distinguishable, and the key turns that uniformity into a diagnosis for the adult ('when a child's answers are all one below the right answer, the fix is the start number, not more practice at counting'). Every corrected total is right. The failure is that five of six problems print an (a) part that verification never touches: problem 6(a) asks the child to 'Tell what Ben did wrong both times' and is recorded as machine-verified with no manual entry, and 2(a), 3(a) and 5(a) ask checkable questions (2 hops; start from 5; start from 7) that appear only in the key's prose, never in the bank or the verifier. final_response.md asserts 'every item has a single numeric answer', which the worksheet contradicts twice. Problem 4, which carries two entries under one id, shows the author knew the right pattern. A third, cosmetic defect: every page of the answer key is headed 'Counting On to Add — Answer Key — Answer Key', because \akheader appends the suffix the argument already contains.
